title: Algebra and algorithm both come from the same person.
description:
Algebra and algorithm both come from the same person. Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, a scholar working in Baghdad in the ninth century.

Wrote 'al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wal-muqabala', 'The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing'.

'Al-jabr', part of that title, meant completing or rejoining broken parts. Carried into Latin, it became 'algebra'. The book's method for solving equations is what made the title worth borrowing.

When 12th-century translators rendered his name in Latin, they wrote it as 'Algoritmi'. That Latinised name became the root of 'algorithm', through a later translation of his separate work on Hindu-Arabic numerals.

He used neither word himself. Translators built both out of his name and his title, centuries after he wrote them.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Khwarizmi - confirms Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote 'al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wal-muqabala' ('The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing'), compiled between about 813 and 833 CE; states the English word 'algebra' comes directly from 'al-jabr' in that title, meaning completion or rejoining; and confirms that when his works were translated into Latin in the 12th century his name was rendered 'Algoritmi', which became the source of the word 'algorithm'.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm - corroborates that the term 'algorithm' derives from 'Algoritmi', the Latinised form of al-Khwarizmi's name, used in the title of the 12th-century Latin translation of his treatise on Hindu-Arabic numerals, 'Algoritmi de numero Indorum'.
